title: The Real Presence in the Eucharist
summary: In the Most Blessed Sacrament of the Eucharist, the body and blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ—and therefore the whole Christ—is truly, really, and substantially present under the appearances of bread and wine, as defined by the Council of Trent and reaffirmed by the magisterium.

blocks.text: Introduction: The Source and Summit of Christian Life

The Eucharist is the source and summit of the Christian life. All other sacraments, ministries, and works of the apostolate are bound up with the Eucharist and are oriented toward it. The Eucharist contains the whole spiritual good of the Church, namely Christ himself, our Pasch and living bread. [CCC 1324-1325]

The doctrine of the Real Presence affirms that after the consecration at Mass, the bread and wine are no longer present, but their appearances remain. Under these appearances, the whole Christ—body, blood, soul, and divinity—is truly, really, and substantially present. This is not a symbolic presence but an ontological reality. [CCC 1373-1374]
I am the living bread which came down from heaven; if any one eats of this bread, he will live for ever; and the bread which I shall give for the life of the world is my flesh.

blocks.title: CCC 1373-1374: True, Real, Substantial Presence
blocks.text: Christ is truly, really, and substantially present in the Eucharist; the whole Christ—body, blood, soul, and divinity—is present under the appearances of bread and wine.
I. Biblical Foundations of the Real Presence

The doctrine of the Real Presence is rooted in Christ's own words at the Last Supper and the Bread of Life discourse in John 6. Jesus did not speak symbolically when he said This is my body and This is my blood; he used literal language that shocked his listeners. Many disciples left him because they understood him literally. [CCC 1334, 1336]

St. Paul affirms the Real Presence when he warns that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of profaning the body and blood of the Lord. He speaks of the Eucharist as a participation in the body and blood of Christ, not merely a memorial. [CCC 1380]

Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed, and broke it, and gave it to the disciples and said, Take, eat; this is my body. And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, Drink of it, all of you; for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

blocks.title: CCC 1334-1336: Christ's Own Words
blocks.text: Christ's words at the Last Supper and in John 6 are literal, not symbolic; many disciples left because they understood him to mean real eating of his flesh.
II. The Council of Trent (1545-1563): Dogmatic Definition

The Protestant Reformers denied the Real Presence, claiming the Eucharist was merely symbolic or a spiritual presence. In response, the Council of Trent defined the dogma of transubstantiation and the Real Presence with precision. Trent anathematized anyone who denied that Christ is truly, really, and substantially present in the Eucharist. [CCC 1376]

Trent taught that by the consecration of the bread and wine, a change takes place in which the whole substance of bread becomes the substance of Christ's body, and the whole substance of wine becomes the substance of his blood. This change is properly called transubstantiation. The appearances of bread and wine remain, but the underlying reality is Christ. [CCC 1376]
Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of profaning the body and blood of the Lord.

blocks.title: Trent Session XIII (1551): Transubstantiation
blocks.text: Trent defined that by consecration, the whole substance of bread and wine becomes Christ's body and blood; this change is properly called transubstantiation, anathematizing deniers.
III. Transubstantiation: Philosophical Explanation

Transubstantiation uses Aristotelian categories of substance and accidents to explain the Eucharistic conversion. Substance refers to what something is in its essence; accidents refer to the sensible properties (taste, appearance, etc.). In the Eucharist, the substance changes while the accidents remain. [CCC 1376]

After consecration, the substance of bread and wine no longer exists; only the accidents remain. The substance is now the body, blood, soul, and divinity of Christ. This is not a physical change detectable by science, but an ontological change known by faith. [CCC 1375-1377]

And he took bread, and when he had given thanks he broke it and gave it to them, saying, This is my body which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me. And likewise the cup after supper, saying, This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.

blocks.title: CCC 1376: Substance and Accidents
blocks.text: Transubstantiation means the substance changes to Christ's body and blood while the accidents (appearances) of bread and wine remain; this is an ontological change known by faith.
IV. The Whole Christ Is Present

The whole Christ—body, blood, soul, and divinity—is present in each species and in every fragment of the consecrated host. Because Christ is risen and glorified, his body and blood cannot be separated; where his body is, there is his blood, soul, and divinity. [CCC 1377]

This is why receiving under one species (bread alone) is still receiving the whole Christ. The Church permits Communion under both species in certain circumstances, but the faithful receive the fullness of Christ under either species alone. Christ is present whole and entire in every particle of the consecrated host. [CCC 1390]
We know that Christ being raised from the dead will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.

blocks.title: CCC 1377: Whole Christ in Each Species
blocks.text: The whole Christ is present in each species and every fragment; receiving under one species is receiving the fullness of Christ, who is risen and indivisible.
V. The Permanence of the Real Presence

The Real Presence of Christ continues as long as the Eucharistic species subsist. This is why the Church reserves the Blessed Sacrament in the tabernacle and adores it outside of Mass. Christ remains present in the consecrated hosts until they are consumed or the appearances cease. [CCC 1377, 1379]

The practice of Eucharistic adoration flows from this doctrine. When we genuflect before the tabernacle or the monstrance, we adore the living Christ truly present. The Church encourages frequent visits to the Blessed Sacrament as an expression of faith and love. [CCC 1378-1379]
And lo, I am with you always, to the close of the age.

blocks.title: CCC 1377-1379: Permanent Presence
blocks.text: Christ's presence continues as long as the Eucharistic species subsist; this is the basis for reservation in the tabernacle and Eucharistic adoration outside Mass.
VI. Vatican II and the Post-Conciliar Magisterium

Vatican Council II (1962-1965) reaffirmed the doctrine of the Real Presence and transubstantiation. The Council taught that in the most blessed sacrament of the Eucharist the body and blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ and, therefore, the whole Christ is truly, really, and substantially contained. [Sacrosanctum Concilium 7]

Pope Paul VI's encyclical Mysterium Fidei (1965) strongly reaffirmed the Real Presence against modern errors that reduced the Eucharist to a mere symbol or presence in the assembly. He insisted that Christ is present in the Eucharist in a manner unique and surpassing all other modes of presence. [Mysterium Fidei 39]
He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.

blocks.title: Vatican II & Mysterium Fidei: Unique Presence
blocks.text: Vatican II and Paul VI reaffirmed that Christ is truly, really, and substantially present in the Eucharist in a manner unique and surpassing all other modes of presence.
VII. The Fruits of Holy Communion

Holy Communion increases our union with Christ and his Church. It preserves and renews the life of grace received in Baptism and strengthens our charity. The Eucharist separates us from sin by cleansing us from venial sins and preserving us from mortal sin. [CCC 1391-1393]

The Eucharist is the antidote to sin and the pledge of future glory. It unites us more closely to Christ, transforms us into him, and commits us to the poor. The Eucharist is the foretaste of the heavenly banquet and the promise of eternal life. [CCC 1394-1396, 1402]
He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day.

blocks.title: CCC 1391-1396: Fruits of Communion
blocks.text: Holy Communion increases union with Christ, preserves grace, cleanses venial sins, strengthens charity, and is the pledge of future glory and resurrection.
VIII. Dispositions for Receiving Communion

To receive Holy Communion worthily, one must be in the state of grace, having confessed any mortal sins in sacramental Confession. One must also observe the Eucharistic fast (one hour before Communion) and approach with reverence and devotion. [CCC 1385, 1415]

Those conscious of mortal sin must not receive Communion without prior sacramental absolution, except in grave necessity when confession is impossible, in which case an act of perfect contrition is required. The Church encourages frequent confession and daily Communion for those in the state of grace. [CCC 1457, 1389]
Let a man examine himself, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.

blocks.title: CCC 1385, 1415: State of Grace
blocks.text: To receive worthily, one must be in the state of grace, observe the Eucharistic fast, and approach with reverence; mortal sin requires prior sacramental Confession.
IX. Eucharistic Adoration and Reservation

The Church reserves the Blessed Sacrament in the tabernacle for several purposes: to bring Viaticum to the sick, to distribute Communion outside Mass, and to enable Eucharistic adoration. The tabernacle should be placed in a worthy, prominent location in the church. [CCC 1379]

Eucharistic adoration is the worship of Christ truly present in the Blessed Sacrament. The Church encourages the faithful to visit the Blessed Sacrament frequently, making acts of faith, hope, and charity. Benediction, exposition, and Forty Hours devotion are traditional forms of Eucharistic piety. [CCC 1378]
Glad songs of salvation are in the tents of the righteous.

blocks.title: CCC 1378-1379: Adoration and Reservation
blocks.text: The Church reserves the Blessed Sacrament for Communion to the sick and Eucharistic adoration; the faithful are encouraged to visit and adore Christ present in the tabernacle.
X. Heresies and Errors Condemned

The Church has condemned various errors regarding the Eucharist. Berengarius (11th century) denied the Real Presence and was forced to recant. The Protestant Reformers (Luther, Calvin, Zwingli) denied transubstantiation, with Zwingli claiming the Eucharist was merely symbolic. [CCC 1376]

Modern errors include reducing the Real Presence to a symbolic or spiritual presence in the assembly, denying the need for Eucharistic adoration, or claiming the presence ceases immediately after Mass. The magisterium continues to affirm the full doctrine of the Real Presence and transubstantiation. [Mysterium Fidei 39]
After this many of his disciples drew back and no longer went about with him. Jesus said to the twelve, Will you also go away?

blocks.title: CCC 1376: Heresies Condemned
blocks.text: The Church condemned Berengarius and the Protestant Reformers for denying the Real Presence and transubstantiation; modern errors reducing the Eucharist to symbol are also rejected.
XI. The Eucharist and the Unity of the Church

The Eucharist is the sacrament of ecclesial unity. Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread. The Eucharist both signifies and effects the unity of the Church. [CCC 1325, 1396]

For this reason, the Church restricts reception of Holy Communion to those in full communion with the Catholic Church. Intercommunion with Protestant communities is not permitted because full ecclesial communion does not yet exist. The Eucharist is both the sign of unity and the means to achieve it. [CCC 1398-1401]
Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.

blocks.title: CCC 1396: Sacrament of Unity
blocks.text: The Eucharist is the sacrament of ecclesial unity; it signifies and effects the unity of the Church, which is why Communion is restricted to those in full communion.
XII. Living Faith in the Real Presence

Faith in the Real Presence requires acts of adoration, thanksgiving, and reparation. The saints had profound devotion to the Eucharist, spending hours in adoration and receiving Communion frequently. St. Thomas Aquinas composed beautiful Eucharistic hymns expressing faith in the Real Presence. [CCC 1380]

We should approach the Eucharist with humility, faith, and love, recognizing that we are receiving the King of kings. Frequent reception of Holy Communion, daily Mass when possible, and regular Eucharistic adoration nourish and strengthen our faith in this great mystery. [CCC 1389, 1418]
Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.

blocks.title: CCC 1380: Eucharistic Piety
blocks.text: Faith in the Real Presence calls for adoration, thanksgiving, and reparation; the saints showed profound Eucharistic devotion, receiving frequently and adoring Christ in the Blessed Sacrament.

blocks.title: Closing Prayer: Anima Christi
blocks.text: Soul of Christ, sanctify me. Body of Christ, save me. Blood of Christ, inebriate me. Water from the side of Christ, wash me. Passion of Christ, strengthen me. O good Jesus, hear me. Within thy wounds hide me. Suffer me not to be separated from thee. From the malicious enemy defend me. In the hour of my death call me. And bid me come unto thee, that with thy saints I may praise thee, for ever and ever. Amen.
